Hull hydrostaticsUpright, at the draught. x from the aft end, KB above the baseline.
Assumptions and limits
  • Buoyancy comes only from the hulls, which are illustrative shapes. Blocks outside a hull, appendages, bulbs and propellers add nothing.
  • The envelope is the box around all blocks, rotated ones included. Overall length, beam and height, and the requirements on them, are read from the envelope, not from the hulls. The hulls are fitted to the blocks below the main deck, so they can be longer or wider than the envelope.
  • The hull drawings and the table of offsets in the PDF come from the same parametric formula as the hydrostatics. They show the illustrative shape the numbers are based on; they are not faired lines.
  • Gross tonnage is an estimate by the 1969 Tonnage Convention from the blocks that count as enclosed spaces. Overlapping blocks count twice. It is not a tonnage certificate.
  • Each block's weight acts at its own centroid. The structure is a percentage of the displacement, spread over the hull volume.
  • Draught is solved with Archimedes' principle: displacement equals the total weight, in a flat sea with one water density.
  • Trim and heel are an exact tilted water plane on the hull shapes, solved so that the volume equals the weight and the centre of buoyancy sits on the vertical through the centre of gravity. All hulls share the plane.
  • The heel needs the vertical centre of gravity, which comes from the block centroids and the structure estimate. A heavy off-centre load on a single hull may have no equilibrium within the range, and then the heel is shown as not found.
  • GM is initial stability (small angles). It is worked out upright and without trim, at the level draught that carries the weight, from the waterplane of the hulls (BM = I / V). The righting-lever curve (GZ) below it heels the hulls with the trim free and ends where the deck edge enters the water: buoyancy above the main deck is not counted. There is no wind, damage, opening or wave effect. The heel above is the equilibrium angle for the loading, not a stability check.
  • Free surface: a block marked Free surface and partly filled is taken as a rectangular tank by its bounding box, which overestimates round or tapered tanks. Only blocks you mark are counted.
  • The basic checks are simple guides (GM at least 0.15 m as in the IMO intact criteria, heel and trim limits as design guides). They are not a stability assessment for class or flag state.
  • The hull checks (blocks outside the hulls, volume below the waterline) use the level draught, also when the trim is shown.
  • Indicative only, for early comparison of arrangements. Not for class or stability documentation.
Total resistance against speed
At the service speed
About this estimate and its limits
  • Holtrop is a method based on statistical regression of model tests and ship trials, for the resistance of displacement ships. It gives a first estimate that is good for comparing designs.
  • It is less accurate for extreme shapes. A warning is shown when L/B (3.9 to 15), B/T (2.1 to 4) or Cp (0.55 to 0.85) are outside the range of the method. Some shapes give no result.
  • The wave resistance grows quickly with speed. Use the curve up to about Froude number 0.45.
  • The inputs are read from the hull at its draught: waterline length and beam, Cb, Cm, Cwp and LCB. The same draught is used forward and aft, so trim is not included. A table hull scales with its size fields, so the result follows them.
  • No appendages are included. The bulbous bow is off unless you tick it: the bulb is then assumed (a default size from the draught) for the resistance only. It is not drawn and does not change the hull shape. Sea water of 1025 kg/m³ is used, whatever the water density is set to.
  • It is for one hull. With several hulls, pick one: the interaction between hulls (catamarans, trimarans) is not included.
  • No propulsion: it is the towing resistance only, with no propeller efficiency, hull efficiency or sea margin. Not for design approval.
  • The formulation follows the ShipLab Holtrop web app (Flor, Monteiro and Gaspar).
Roll

Sea state

Limits
About this estimate and its limits
  • Closed-form estimate of Jensen, Mansour and Olsen (2004): the ship is a box of the waterline length, the draught and a breadth of waterline breadth times Cb. The charts give the response per wave frequency, for the wave amplitude set. A first estimate for comparing designs, not a strip theory or model test.
  • Inputs come from the hull at its draught; GM from the Hydrostatics tab unless typed; speed from the Resistance tab. The centre of gravity is at midlength, and the position is in % of half the length (0 the centre of gravity, 100 the bow). One hull at a time: seakeeping of multihulls (catamarans, trimarans) is not possible.
  • Sea state: Pierson-Moskowitz or JONSWAP spectrum from Hs, Tz or Tp, the peak factor and the duration. Each response gives the RMS, the significant amplitude (twice the RMS) and the most probable maximum (Rayleigh peaks). One sea state and one heading; no scatter diagram. The bending moment is not included, as it is non-linear.
  • Limits (RMS): vertical acceleration in g, roll and pitch in degrees, from NORDFORSK and NATO presets, all editable. The limiting Hs is the wave height at which the response reaches the limit; the response grows in proportion to Hs. Lateral acceleration is not checked (no sway).
  • Motion sickness: MSDV is the square root of the duration times the RMS vertical acceleration at the position, weighted by the ISO 2631-1 filter Wf, and VI = MSDV/3 in %. Defined for 20 minutes to 6 hours. Presets: ABS 30 and 45 m/s1.5 for 6 h.
  • Outside the limits of the method (pink, with a warning): B/T from 1 to 6 (roll); Froude number below 0.3 and Cb of at least 0.6 (bending moment); the prismatic length ratio above Cwp; beam waves; roll in waves that overtake the ship. Pink bands: heave for waves longer than the ship, pitch near wave length equal to ship length above Fn 0.2, roll near resonance. The paper compares ships at Fn 0.13 to 0.84. Deep water, heave and pitch 90 degrees out of phase.
  • Bending moment: wave-induced vertical moment at midship, in 106 N·m. Sea water 1025 kg/m³.
  • Formulation follows the ShipLab ship motion web app. References: Jensen, Mansour and Olsen (2004), Ocean Engineering 31, 61–85; Stevens and Parsons (2002), Marine Technology 39(1), 29–47; ISO 2631-1 (1997); Taylor (2023), Stellenbosch University.

Longitudinal strength

Midship section

Thickness in mm, spacing in m, profile dimensions in mm.

Local scantlings

Steel weight

About this check and its limits
  • First check to the DNV Rules for Ships, Pt.3 Ch.2 (January 2015, ships under 100 m). Educational, not a class check. A warning is given above 100 m.
  • Single hull only. The rule length is 96% of the waterline length, with the AP at the aft end of the waterline.
  • Stillwater load: block weights (spread uniformly over each block’s length) plus the structure, spread with the hull section area, against the buoyancy at the floating position of the Float state. Moment positive in sagging; the end residual is removed linearly.
  • Rule bending moments of Sec.4 B and the section modulus of C101 and C104. Where the calculated stillwater moment is below the rule value MSO, the rule value is used.
  • Midship section: box with sides of constant thickness, no bilge or sheer strake, no girders or transverses; net thicknesses as entered. Longitudinals with the plate flange of one stiffener spacing.
  • Local scantlings at midship (ks = 2): bottom, side and strength deck plating and longitudinals, the keel plate and the inner bottom minimum. Load points at half breadth. Not covered: bulkheads, floors, girders, frames, tanks, buckling (Sec.12), shear strength, fatigue, superstructures.
  • Steel weight: net section area times 7.85 t/m³ times the hull length times the allowance factor. A rough estimate.
